description:
Mga Bisaya with Big Dreams.

Bisdak Syndicate is an interdisciplinary team of students from Physics, Computer Science, Communication, and Engineering across different state universities, all driven by a shared objective to build practical solutions for local citizens in general.
summary: umaWISE (uma is the Bisaya word for farm) is a map-based web app that helps farmers in Misamis Oriental, Philippines decide what to plant and when, using NASA Earth observation records for their own location. A farmer searches for a barangay, taps a point, or draws a box over their land on a satellite map. umaWISE then shows the latest NASA POWER weather and soil-wetness records, compares recent rainfall with the same months in past years, reads the elevation and slope of the land from NASA SRTM, and checks eight locally grown crops against published crop requirements for the chosen planting month. Color-coded pins give a quick green, orange, or red reading across the province, Google Gemini rewrites the calculated results in plain language, and opt-in SMS alerts reach farmers on basic phones when the records show dry spells, low rainfall, dry soil, or heavy rain. The challenge asks how farms can adapt as conditions shift. umaWISE answers by turning long satellite records into guidance a smallholder can read in a minute, while staying honest that it describes recorded conditions and is not a weather forecast.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

umaWISE is a web map tool that gives Misamis Oriental farmers weather, terrain, soil, and crop guidance for their barangay, a single map point, or a custom area they draw. A typical visit goes like this:

  1. Find a location: The farmer searches for a town or barangay, or taps directly on the map. The base map is Esri satellite imagery, so farmers can recognize their own land instead of reading coordinates.
  2. Select a point or draw an area: Color-coded pins across the province give a first reading (green, orange, or red). The farmer can also draw a box over a farm to see its coordinates, its size in hectares, and the date of the newest record.
  3. Read the map rating: Each pin is rated on two checks, and the worse one sets the color. Rain: the total of the latest three complete months (GPM IMERG) is compared with the same months in every earlier year. Lower than in 4 of 5 past years is a caution; lower than in 9 of 10 is marked hard. Land: slope from NASA SRTM. 18% and steeper is a caution, 30% and steeper is marked hard.
  4. Review the Historical Analysis: A report for the selected point compares recent rainfall with past years, counts dry spells and heavy-rain days, tests for a long-term trend, and shows ground elevation and slope. On slopes of 18% or more it points the farmer to contour planting to limit soil erosion.
  5. Check Near-Live Weather (NASA POWER): A weather card shows the latest daily records for the location: air temperature, humidity, wind speed, and rainfall, with a strip of the last seven recorded days. These are near-real-time records, and the card says clearly that it is not a forecast.
  6. Check Soil Condition (NASA POWER): A soil card turns the modelled root-zone wetness index into a percentage with a plain label (Dry, Slightly moist, Moderately moist, or Wet) and shows surface temperature.
  7. See which crops fit: The farmer picks a planting month. umaWISE checks corn, rice, cassava, peanut, tomato, cabbage, potato, and carrot against the recorded rainfall, temperature, and elevation of that place, using requirement ranges from the FAO EcoCrop database. Each crop is labelled Fits, Fits with limits, Does not fit, or Not assessed, and the card names the reason.
  8. Get a plain-language explanation: Google Gemini rewrites the calculated findings into short, simple advice. Gemini only receives numbers the server has already computed. It never supplies data, its text is labelled as AI-written, and every result still works without it.
  9. Receive SMS alerts: A farmer can register a mobile number, confirm it with a one-time code, and choose which alerts to get: many dry days in a row, low rain over 30 days, soil wetness lower than usual, evaporation higher than rain, or a heavy rain day. Thresholds, quiet hours, and how often to be messaged are the farmer’s choice, and the subscription can be deleted at any time.

For corn, the backend also runs a deeper water check based on FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56: it computes daily reference evapotranspiration from NASA POWER weather and compares crop water use with rainfall across past seasons. Official PAGASA seasonal outlook tables are read as separate context and are never mixed into the NASA figures.

BENEFITS

  • Advice for the place, not the province: Results change with the selected point, its rainfall history, and its slope, so a coastal plain and an upland farm in Claveria are not treated the same.
  • Easy to read: Satellite imagery, three-color pins, and plain words such as "Moderately moist" and "Fits with limits" replace technical charts and units.
  • Reaches basic phones: SMS alerts work on any mobile phone and do not need mobile data, which matters in upland areas with weak signal.
  • Better crop choices and soil protection: Multi-year rainfall records, current soil wetness, and slope warnings reduce guesswork about what to plant and where erosion control is needed.
  • Less loss and waste: Early notice of dry spells and heavy rain helps farmers time planting, watering, and harvesting.
  • Honest about its limits: Every card states its data source and coverage. When records are missing the app says "not assessed" instead of guessing, and it directs farmers to PAGASA for weather warnings and to their Municipal Agriculture Office for final crop decisions.

INTENDED IMPACT

The impact of umaWISE unfolds in three stages. In the short term, individual farmers make better-informed planting decisions, adopt slope-safe practices, and get early notice when the records turn unusually dry or wet. In the medium term, agricultural cooperatives, local government units (LGUs), and Municipal Agriculture Offices can use the same map to advise their communities with one shared, sourced picture of local conditions. In the long term, umaWISE aims to move Misamis Oriental toward data-driven, climate-resilient farming and to serve as a model that other provinces can copy, because the NASA datasets behind it cover the whole country.

TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND SOFTWARE

umaWISE used the following programming languages and tools to take this innovation into reality:

  • Python: used for the backend and for data analysis. The API is built with FastAPI and served by Uvicorn. pandas cleans and summarizes the NASA POWER exports, rasterio reads the SRTM elevation and slope rasters, pdfplumber reads the PAGASA outlook tables, and httpx calls the NASA POWER API and the Gemini API.
  • TypeScript and React, packaged with Vite: used for the web app. The map is built with Leaflet and react-leaflet, and icons come from Lucide. The layout is responsive, from phone to desktop.
  • Supabase (PostgreSQL): the cloud database for the deployed app. It stores the prepared climate records, the crop requirement table, and SMS subscriptions in a private schema. SQLite is used for local development.
  • UniSMS: the Philippine SMS gateway that delivers verification codes and alerts. The backend defaults to a safe dry-run mode, so no message is sent unless live sending is switched on.
  • Google Gemini API: writes the optional plain-language explanations.
  • Heroku: hosts the API and the built web app.
  • Git and GitHub: version control and the public code repository.
  • Figma: interface design and the design system.
  • Hardware: none beyond the team’s laptops. umaWISE needs no sensors or field equipment, which keeps it free for farmers to use.

CREATIVITY OF THIS PROJECT

Designed with the farmers of Misamis Oriental in mind, umaWISE brings satellite Earth observations, multi-year climate records, and terrain analysis together on a single, familiar screen: a satellite photo of the farmer’s own land. The creative choice was to translate, not to add more charts. A rainfall percentile becomes a green, orange, or red pin. A root-zone wetness index becomes "Moderately moist". Crop requirement ranges become "Fits with limits", with the reason beside it. Gemini is used as a translator and not as an oracle: it explains numbers that the server has already calculated, so the advice stays traceable to NASA data. SMS then carries the same findings to growers who have no smartphone or steady internet.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

  • Microclimates and topography: Elevation and slope change quickly from the coastal plains to upland Claveria, which alters temperature, soil moisture, and erosion risk. This is why terrain is checked beside rainfall.
  • Connectivity and devices: Rural communities often have weak internet and basic phones, so SMS alerts and a lightweight, mobile-friendly web app were prioritized.
  • Language and literacy: Color-coded indicators, plain-language labels, and short AI explanations keep the tool usable without technical training.
  • Data resolution and honesty: NASA POWER cells are about 55 by 70 km, IMERG rainfall cells about 11 km, and SRTM terrain about 90 m. The app names the source and scale of every figure, labels past records as past records, and never presents them as farm-level measurements or forecasts.
  • Local crops and evidence: The crop list covers crops grown in Northern Mindanao: corn, rice, cassava, peanut, and highland vegetables (tomato, cabbage, potato, carrot). Requirement ranges come from FAO EcoCrop, and farming-practice notes come from published studies on Claveria and Bukidnon.
  • Privacy and consent: SMS is opt-in only. Numbers are verified with a one-time code, shown masked, protected by quiet hours and send limits, and removable by the farmer.
  • Responsible use of AI: AI text is labelled, receives only calculated indicators, and cannot change any number. If the AI service fails, the calculated results are still shown.

RECOMMENDATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

  • Filter out non-farm areas: Because of the time constraint of the hackathon, the map currently rates every point inside the province. Housing, the sea, and built structures in general should be filtered out so that only cropland, which is the scope of umaWISE, is considered. A land-cover mask would do this.
  • Bisaya interface: Add a full Bisaya translation, with local crop names, checked by native speakers.
  • Offline use: Make the app installable with offline caching for areas where the signal drops.
  • More crops: Extend the crop table to other crops important to the province, such as coconut, banana, cacao, and coffee.
  • Local support directory: Add map markers for cooperatives, agricultural stations, and Municipal Agriculture Offices.
  • Field validation: Test the ratings and crop results with farmers and agricultural technicians before wider use.
  • Data Enrichment: Integrate updated, high-resolution datasets—particularly topographic data—to improve the accuracy and analytical depth of the dashboard.
  • Nationwide Scalability: Scale the spatial analysis beyond Misamis Oriental to cover the entire Philippines.
  • Interactive Visual Filtering: Implement a map filter allowing users to isolate red, yellow, and green priority zones for a cleaner, more user-friendly display.
  • Context-Aware Backend Filtering: Configure the backend to distinguish between urban, coastal, and agricultural zones, preventing farm-specific criteria from being misapplied to city areas.
  • Crop Diversification: Broaden the model's scope to include fruit-bearing crops alongside traditional cash crops for more comprehensive recommendations.
